title: Brakes squeal
metaDesc: Brakes squealing or squeaking? Answer a few quick questions to see if it's worn pads, rust or vibration, how urgent it is, and what to tell your mechanic.
intro: Most brake squeal is a warning, not an emergency. The trick is telling a normal morning squeak from worn-out pads or a brake that's sticking. Answer the questions below and we'll point you to the most likely cause and how soon to act.
safety: If the brake pedal feels soft, sinks toward the floor, or the car takes longer to stop, stop driving and get help.
If the red brake warning light is on, don't drive until the brakes are checked.
If you smell burning or see smoke from a wheel, pull over safely and let it cool. Don't keep driving.

If smoke continues, you see flames or you suspect a fire, pull over safely and switch off the vehicle. Get everyone out, move at least 100 feet away and clear of traffic, and call 911. Stay away from the vehicle.

q_other_signs.q: Along with the squeal, is any of this happening?
q_other_signs.help: These signs tell us whether this is more than a noise. Pick the most serious one that fits.

opts.a: The pedal feels soft or sinks, the car takes longer to stop, or the red brake light is on
A burning smell, smoke, or one wheel is much hotter than the others after driving
There's also a grinding or metal-scraping sound
The car pulls to one side when I brake

q_when.q: When do you hear the squeal?

opts.a: Only on the first few stops in the morning, or after rain or a car wash, then it goes away
Almost every time I brake, and it's been getting more frequent
A steady squeal or chirp while driving, even when I'm not braking
Only when I brake lightly; firm stops are quiet
Mostly when backing up or creeping along at very low speed
It started right after new brakes were put on

q_pad_age.q: When were the brake pads last replaced?
q_pad_age.help: Check your service records or the last shop invoice. Pads usually last a few years, but city driving and heavy loads wear them faster.

opts.a: Recently, within the last year or so
It's been a while, or not since I've owned the car

result.title: The brakes may not be stopping the car properly
result.now: Don't drive it. Park it somewhere safe and have it towed, or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If you're on the road now, slow down gently, use a lower gear if you can, and pull over somewhere safe.
If the brake fluid reservoir under the hood is low or there's a wet spot near a wheel, mention that to the shop. It points to a leak.
result.why: A squeal by itself is usually a wear warning. A soft or sinking pedal, longer stops or the red brake light usually mean the braking system itself has a problem, such as low fluid, a leak or badly worn parts. That's a safety risk, not just a noise.

causes.name: Brake fluid leak or low fluid
causes.clues: A soft or sinking pedal, the red brake light, or a damp spot near a wheel or on the ground.

causes.name: Pads worn down to metal
causes.clues: The squeal has been there a while, and now stopping takes more effort.

causes.name: Air in the brake lines or a failing master cylinder
causes.clues: A spongy pedal that slowly sinks while you hold it at a stop.
causes.against: Less likely if the pedal feels firm and the only change is noise.

you: With the engine off, look at the brake fluid reservoir level. Don't open it if the engine is hot.
Look for wet spots on the inside of the wheels or under the car.
shop: Brake system inspection, including pad thickness and rotors
Master cylinder and brake line test

result.title: A brake may be sticking and dragging on one wheel
result.now: Pull over safely and switch off the vehicle. If you suspect a fire, including smoke that continues or visible flames, get everyone at least 100 feet away and clear of traffic and call 911. If there is only a hot smell, stay clear of the wheel and arrange a tow or mobile brake inspection before driving again.
if: If the parking brake was left partly on, release it fully and let the brakes cool. Have them checked before relying on them. Overheated brakes can fade, and the fluid may need testing.
result.why: A brake that stays partly applied keeps rubbing, which creates heat, noise and a burning smell. The heat can damage the brake and wheel bearing and make the brakes fade when you need them.

causes.name: Sticking caliper or caliper slide pins
causes.clues: One wheel is much hotter or dustier than the others, and the car may pull to that side.

causes.name: Parking brake not fully releasing
causes.clues: The heat is at a rear wheel, or the parking brake lever or button feels odd.

causes.name: Collapsed brake hose
causes.clues: The brake releases slowly, and the problem comes and goes.

you: Make sure the parking brake is fully released.
Notice which wheel smells or feels hotter from a distance. Don't touch it.
shop: Wheel temperature comparison after a test drive
Brake hose and parking brake check

result.title: The pads may be worn down to metal
result.now: Get the brakes inspected before driving further. If the pads are down to metal, braking may take more force and can get worse quickly. Have it towed or ask a mobile mechanic to check it where it's parked.
if: If the pedal feels soft, the car pulls, or stops take longer, don't try to move the car. Have it towed.

If the noise only happened on the first stops after rain and then went away, it may have been surface rust. Our grinding-brakes guide covers that, but have the pads looked at before relying on the brakes.
result.why: Squealing that turns into grinding often means the pad material is nearly or fully gone and metal is touching the rotor. That reduces braking and can quickly damage the rotor. A shop will measure the pads and rotors to see what's actually needed.

causes.name: Brake pads worn through
causes.clues: The squeal came first, then grinding started. It happens on most stops.
causes.against: Less likely if the pads were replaced recently.

causes.name: Stone or debris caught in the brake
causes.clues: A sudden scraping sound after driving on gravel.

causes.name: Rusted or damaged rotor
causes.clues: The car sat for a long time, or you feel a pulse in the pedal.

you: Look through the wheel spokes at the brake pads. If you see very little pad left against the rotor, tell the shop.
Notice whether the noise happens on every stop or only some.

result.title: One side may be braking harder than the other
result.now: Get the brakes checked in the next day or two, and keep driving to a minimum until then. Leave extra stopping room and avoid hard stops where you can.
if: If the pull is strong, gets worse, or comes with a burning smell, stop driving and have it towed.
If you see wet fluid near one wheel, or the pedal feels soft, don't drive it. A leaking caliper or hose can cause a pull.
If the pull only happens when you're not braking, it's more likely tire pressure or alignment.
result.why: A squeal plus a pull to one side often means one brake isn't working the same as the other. A sticking caliper or contaminated pads on one side can do this, and it can make the car harder to control in a hard stop.

causes.name: Sticking caliper or slide pins
causes.clues: One wheel gets hotter or dustier than the other.

causes.name: Uneven pad wear or contaminated pads
causes.clues: Oil or brake fluid near one wheel, or one side was serviced and the other wasn't.

causes.name: Tire or alignment problem
causes.clues: The car also drifts when you're not braking, or one tire looks low.
causes.against: Less likely if it only pulls while braking.

you: Check the tire pressures on both sides.
Notice whether it pulls only when braking or all the time.
shop: Pad and rotor wear comparison side to side

result.title: Often a thin layer of surface rust on the rotors
result.now: If the squeal fades within the first few stops, it's often just surface rust. Brake gently for the first few stops and listen for whether it clears.
if: If the squeal stays after the first few miles, or starts happening on every stop, have the brakes checked.
If you hear grinding, not just squealing, have the brakes inspected soon.
If the pedal feels soft or sinks, the car takes longer to stop, the red brake light comes on, or you smell burning from a wheel, stop driving and have it towed.
result.why: Brake rotors are bare iron, so moisture leaves a light film of rust overnight or after rain. The first few stops scrape it off, which can squeal or squeak briefly. This is common and usually clears up quickly.

causes.name: Light surface rust from moisture
causes.clues: Happens after the car sits overnight, after rain or a wash, and goes away quickly.
causes.against: If it lasts all day, something else is going on.

causes.name: Moisture on the pads
causes.clues: Worse in humid or damp weather.

you: Notice whether the squeal is gone after the first few stops.
If the car sits for weeks at a time, drive it more often or have the rotors looked at for heavy rust.
shop: Rotor inspection if the noise doesn't clear

result.title: The brake pad wear indicator may be telling you the pads are low
result.now: Book a brake inspection within the next week. Ask the shop to measure the pads and the rotors so you know what's actually needed.
if: If the squeal turns into grinding, get the brakes inspected before driving further. That can mean metal is touching metal.
If the pedal feels soft or sinks, the car takes longer to stop, the red brake light comes on, or you smell burning from a wheel, stop driving and have it towed.
If the car pulls to one side when braking, get it checked within a day or two.
result.why: Many brake pads have a small metal tab that scrapes the rotor when the pad gets thin, making a high-pitched squeal on purpose. It's a built-in reminder. Acting now usually means just pads; waiting can mean rotors too.

causes.name: Pad wear indicator touching the rotor
causes.clues: A high-pitched squeal that's become steady, and the pads haven't been changed in a while.
causes.against: Less likely if the pads are nearly new.

causes.name: Worn or glazed pads
causes.clues: The brakes feel a little less grabby than before.

causes.name: Stone or bent dust shield rubbing
causes.clues: A scraping squeal that started suddenly, even when you're not braking.

you: Look through the wheel spokes at the pad thickness on the brake caliper.
Check your records for when the pads were last replaced.
shop: Pad thickness measurement on all wheels

result.title: Often pad vibration, from missing shims, lube or glazed pads
result.now: Book a brake check when convenient. Ask the shop to look at the pad shims, clips and lubrication, not just pad thickness.
if: If the squeal gets louder, becomes constant, or turns into grinding, get it checked soon.
If the pedal feels soft or sinks, the car takes longer to stop, the red brake light comes on, or you smell burning from a wheel, stop driving and have it towed.
If the pads were just replaced, call the shop that did the work first.
result.why: Brake squeal is often a high-frequency vibration between the pad and rotor. Light braking is where it shows up most. Worn shims, dry contact points, glazed pads or certain pad materials can cause it even when there's plenty of pad left.

causes.name: Missing, worn or dry shims and contact points
causes.clues: Squeals on light stops, quiet on firm ones, and the pads aren't worn.

causes.name: Glazed pads or rotors
causes.clues: Hard braking down hills or a stuck brake in the past. The rotor may look shiny.

causes.name: Pad material
causes.clues: Some harder pads are naturally noisier, especially when cold.

you: Notice whether light or firm braking makes the noise.
Check whether one wheel seems to be the source by listening with a window down at low speed.

result.title: Low-speed squeak is often normal pad noise
result.now: Look through the wheels to make sure the pads aren't thin, and keep an ear on it. If it doesn't change, mention it at your next service.
if: If the noise starts happening at normal speeds or gets louder, book a brake check.
If you also hear grinding, have the brakes inspected soon.
If the pedal feels soft or sinks, the car takes longer to stop, the red brake light comes on, or you smell burning from a wheel, stop driving and have it towed.
result.why: Many pads squeak a little when you're barely moving, especially when reversing or creeping in traffic. The pads can shift slightly when you change direction, and some pad materials are just noisier at low speed.

causes.name: Normal pad noise at low speed
causes.clues: Only when backing up or creeping, and braking feels normal.

causes.name: Pads shifting when the car changes direction
causes.clues: A single click or squeak right after you switch from Reverse to Drive.

causes.name: Early pad wear
causes.clues: The pads haven't been replaced in a long time.

you: Look at pad thickness through the wheel spokes.
Notice if it only happens in Reverse.
shop: Brake inspection at your next service

result.title: New brakes may need breaking in, or something may need adjusting
result.now: Give the new brakes a few days of normal driving to bed in. If the squeal is still there, call the shop that did the work and have them recheck it.
if: If the pedal feels soft or different, the car pulls, or you hear grinding, don't drive it. Call the shop that did the work and have them check it or arrange a tow.
If you see wet fluid at a wheel, or the red brake light comes on, don't drive it.
If the noise started after old shims or clips were reused, ask the shop to check those.
result.why: New pads need some normal stops to bed into the rotor and can squeak at first. If the noise continues, common reasons are missing shims or lube, pads that don't suit the rotors, or old rotors that weren't replaced or resurfaced.

causes.name: Pads still bedding in
causes.clues: The brakes are only a few days old and the noise is fading.

causes.name: Missing shims, clips or lubricant
causes.clues: The noise is constant and isn't fading.

causes.name: Old rotors not replaced or resurfaced
causes.clues: Only the pads were changed.

you: Check the invoice to see whether rotors and hardware were replaced.
Notice whether the noise is getting better or worse.
shop: Recheck of pad fit, shims and clips

result.title: Have the brakes inspected to find the source
result.now: Book a brake inspection when convenient. Note when the squeal happens so you can tell the shop.
if: If the pedal feels soft, the car takes longer to stop, or you hear grinding, stop driving and have it towed.
If you smell burning from a wheel or the car pulls when braking, stop driving and have it checked.
If it gets louder or more frequent, move the appointment up.
result.why: Brake squeal has several common causes, from harmless moisture to worn pads. When it's hard to say when it happens, a look at the pads and rotors usually narrows it down.

causes.name: Pad wear indicator
causes.clues: The pads haven't been replaced in a while.

causes.name: Pad vibration or glazing
causes.clues: Squeals on some stops but not others.

causes.name: Surface rust
causes.clues: Mostly in the morning or after rain.

you: Record a short video with sound when it happens. It helps the shop.
Look at pad thickness through the wheel spokes.
